text.p: Britain's biggest furniture retailer MFI Furniture Group Plc said on Tuesday sales had picked up since the general election in May and was hopeful the benefit of windfall spending from building society flotations was still to come.
Chief executive John Randall said although its was difficult to come up with a single reason for the upturn in sales since April, it seemed to be a pre-election and post-election phenomenon.
"From about November through to the end of April business was deteriorating, but since the election's out of the way it's improved," he said in a telephone interview.

He said it was a little early for MFI's customers to be spending the cash received via the demutualisation of home loan groups such as Halifax. The current sales upturn was likely to be the result of business that had been in the pipeline for the past six months.
"Most of our customers are making a very considered purchase, for many of them it takes several months," Randall said. "My hope is that the windfalls are still to come."
He said the biggest factor driving the recovery in sales growth, which had dropped to two to three percent in March and April, was an upturn in consumer confidence.
The housing market, which inevitably affects MFI's business, had seen a gradual improvement, but this was confined to the south east of England and the top end of the market, he said.
"I think the biggest single factor is confidence," Randall said, "I think that's what's been lacking until relatively recently -- the last couple of months."
He was sceptical about the view that the consumer economy is already overheating, prompting calls for measures to curb consumer spending in the new Labour government's first budget on Wednesday.
"I find this talk about overheating a little bizarre...we've had a couple of good months but I wouldn't suggest that the months prior to that were particularly good."
Randall said it was nevertheless encouraging that sales in the past couple of months had managed to beat those of the same period last year, when they were ahead by 15 percent.

MFI's new Homeworks format was continuing to perform well, achieving a 10 percent additional growth in sales, Randall said. The company has converted half of its 186 stores and hopes to complete the process over the next two years.
The group said the new-style stores were attracting and retaining a broader range of customers, including more younger shoppers.

Randall said the conversion programme, plus a large warehouse pilot scheme, had meant additional costs in terms of payroll and overheads during the year. But he predicted costs would come down over the next 18 months as a result of the new warehouse system and other efficiencies.
The strong pound helped MFI's lower manufacturing costs, but hit earnings from France, where it has 99 stores trading under the Hygena name.

France broke even after making a small profit in the previous year. Randall said more stringent planning restrictions had forced the group to switch to smaller stores which are not affected by the new planning regulations.
This will allow the group to speed up expansion, with the aim of having 200 stores in the next two to three years.
The group also has five trial stores in Spain, and has other European countries in its sites, but Randall would not say which ones.

Earlier MFI reported a 21 percent increase in profits for the year to end April 1997 to 70.3 million stg. The group's shares were 7.5 pence lower at 127.5 by 0850 GMT. --Jane Merriman, London Newsroom+44 171 542 7717
